1. Plain-Language Explanation of Trust Boundaries

This architecture separates untrusted browsers/API callers, Next.js server route handlers, Supabase Auth/PostgREST, and PostgreSQL data/RLS, with the following enforcement layers:

Browser / Caller → Next.js API Routes (/api/services, /api/bookings)

Everything coming from the browser or HTTP clients (GET/POST payloads, Authorization headers, service_id, client_email) is untrusted.

TypeScript guarantees (ServiceCreateInput, BookingCreateInput, PublicService) exist only at compile time and are erased at runtime; they do not protect JSON APIs or database responses.

Runtime validation (Zod schemas in src/schemas/service.ts and src/schemas/booking.ts) enforces strict shapes (.strict()), string lengths, formats, and numeric bounds only for traffic passing through the Next.js routes.

Next.js Server Modules → Credential Isolation (supabaseServer.ts vs supabase-server.ts)

Both files use import 'server-only' so keys cannot be bundled into browser code.

Ordinary public/authenticated routes (/api/services, /api/bookings) use createSupabaseUserClient() with the anon/publishable key, never getSupabaseAdmin() (SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY). Thus, Next.js never bypasses RLS for public or provider writes.

Real Authentication vs Database Authorization (RLS & GRANTs)

In POST /api/services, real authentication occurs when supabase.auth.getUser(bearer[1]) verifies the JWT against Supabase Auth (GoTrue).

That same Authorization header is forwarded to PostgREST so PostgreSQL evaluates (select auth.uid()) inside Row-Level Security (RLS) policies.

Because SUPABASE_ANON_KEY/SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY is inherently public in Supabase architectures, attackers can also call PostgREST directly, bypassing Next.js routes and Zod entirely. Therefore, PostgreSQL GRANTs, CHECK constraints, and RLS policies are the ultimate security boundary:

anon can read approved + coverage_active services and INSERT bookings for those services (with no SELECT grant on bookings, protecting client PII).

authenticated providers/merchants can read/insert draft services and read bookings only for their own services.

service_role is isolated for privileged server/admin operations (not exercised in the shown routes).

2. Concrete Findings (Up to Five)
Finding 1: Any authenticated user can self-assign provider or merchant role via direct PostgREST INSERT

Location: supabase/migrations/20261118000700_midterm_profile_roles.sql lines 7–10; supabase/migrations/20261118000400_restore_backend_contracts_rls.sql line 141.

Attack or Failure: 004 grants SELECT, INSERT on public.profiles to authenticated, and 007's backend_profile_insert_non_admin allows any authenticated user to insert a row for id = (select auth.uid()) with role in ('client', 'provider', 'merchant'). A standard user without a profile row yet can bypass any Next.js onboarding UI and call PostgREST directly (POST /rest/v1/profiles) to claim 'provider' or 'merchant', unlocking POST /api/services, backend_service_provider_*, and backend_booking_provider_read.

Uncertainty: Omitted code may include an auth.users signup trigger that pre-creates a 'client' profile row (which would cause a primary-key conflict on a second insert), or self-serve provider signup may be intentional since services still start in 'draft'.

Severity: Medium (blocks 'admin' escalation and self-publishing, but allows unauthorized provider onboarding and draft-table spam if providers are meant to be vetted).

Smallest Safe Fix: Restrict backend_profile_insert_non_admin to role = 'client' (preserving existing rows), and promote accounts to 'provider'/'merchant' only via an admin/verification workflow using service_role. (If self-serve provider registration is required, require an admin-controlled verification flag in profiles before services RLS allows creation.)

Verification Test (Fictional Data): Authenticate a fresh fictional user new-user@example.invalid with no profiles row; execute a direct PostgREST INSERT into public.profiles with { id: <uid>, role: 'provider' }. Confirm PostgreSQL rejects it with 42501, role: 'client' succeeds, and POST /api/services with that user's JWT returns 403.

Finding 2: Providers can alter or delete 'suspended' services—bypassing admin moderation and cascading bookings

Location: supabase/migrations/20261118000400_restore_backend_contracts_rls.sql lines 198–214 (backend_service_provider_update, backend_service_provider_delete); supabase/migrations/20261029140000_exam_services_persistence.sql line 44.

Attack or Failure: Both backend_service_provider_update and backend_service_provider_delete grant providers access when status in ('draft', 'suspended'). If an administrator suspends a listing (status = 'suspended') for fraud or policy violations, the owning provider can immediately UPDATE status back to 'draft' (clearing the suspension state) or DELETE the service—which also triggers on delete cascade on public.bookings (20261029140000 line 44), wiping out booking records and evidence.

Severity: Medium (moderation/integrity bypass and unintended PII/audit-record destruction).

Smallest Safe Fix: Restrict backend_service_provider_update (with check, and ideally using) and backend_service_provider_delete to status = 'draft' so providers cannot modify, unsuspended-reset, or delete 'suspended' listings. Consider changing bookings.service_id foreign-key behavior from on delete cascade to on delete restrict for services that have bookings.

Verification Test (Fictional Data): Seed a fictional service owned by provider-1@example.invalid with status = 'suspended' and one linked booking for client-1@example.invalid. Using provider-1's JWT against PostgREST, attempt PATCH (status = 'draft') and DELETE on that service; confirm both fail with 42501 and the booking row remains intact.

Finding 3: Strict creation-schema validation on GET /api/services lets one legacy/non-conforming row take down all service discovery (502)

Location: src/app/api/services/route.ts lines 8–24; src/schemas/service.ts lines 3–18.

Attack or Failure: PublicServiceSchema extends ServiceCreateSchema (requiring title 5–200 chars, JS number hourly_rate, duration_minutes >= 15, coverage_radius_miles >= 1), and ServiceListResponseSchema validates the entire array at once. If any single approved, active row in public.services violates a creation rule (e.g., a legacy row with a 4-char title, a direct PostgREST insert if omitted SQL constraints are looser, or a numeric column serialized as a string by a driver/proxy), safeParse fails the whole payload and GET /api/services returns HTTP 502 for every visitor. Additionally, GET /api/services lacks .limit()/pagination.

Uncertainty: Omitted lines 1–41 of 20261029140000_exam_services_persistence.sql may already enforce identical CHECK constraints on services, though legacy/null/type-serialization mismatches can still occur.

Severity: Medium (availability / DoS on public catalog discovery).

Smallest Safe Fix: Decouple PublicServiceSchema from ServiceCreateSchema (validate structural types and safely coerce numeric fields for existing rows rather than re-enforcing creation constraints on read), filter/log any malformed row individually instead of failing the entire list with 502, and add .limit()/pagination.

Verification Test (Fictional Data): Seed two approved, active fictional services—one valid ("Standard Lawn Trim") and one legacy/short title ("Trim", if DB permits, or mock a string "45.00" hourly_rate from PostgREST). Call GET /api/services and verify it returns 200 with valid service data rather than 502.

Finding 4: Unthrottled public booking insertion and Zod/SQL contract mismatches across API and direct PostgREST

Location: src/app/api/bookings/route.ts lines 36–44; src/schemas/booking.ts lines 5–10; supabase/migrations/20261029140000_exam_services_persistence.sql lines 45–47; supabase/migrations/20261118000400_restore_backend_contracts_rls.sql lines 146, 227–231.

Attack or Failure:

POST /api/bookings has no rate limiting, bot protection, or duplicate-submission controls, and 004 grants anon direct INSERT on public.bookings. Attackers can flood bookings or spam providers with bookings referencing arbitrary unverified client_email addresses via either /api/bookings or PostgREST directly.

BookingCreateSchema allows any calendar date (including past dates like 1900-01-01), and SQL has no requested_date bound or btrim(notes) check—so direct PostgREST inserts accept whitespace-only notes (' ').

Conversely, Zod .email() accepts RFC-valid addresses containing characters like ! or non-ASCII letters that SQL's client_email regex rejects (23514), returning a generic "Could not submit booking request." instead of field validation errors.

Severity: Medium (abuse/DoS vector and client-bypassable data contracts).

Smallest Safe Fix: Add rate limiting/challenge protection on POST /api/bookings; add SQL CHECK constraints (char_length(btrim(notes)) between 10 and 2000 and a requested_date lower bound, added NOT VALID to preserve legacy rows); enforce requested_date >= current_date in BookingCreateSchema and align its client_email check with the SQL regex.

Verification Test (Fictional Data):

Submit { service_id: <approved>, client_email: 'client@example.invalid', requested_date: '2020-01-01', notes: 'Past date check' } to POST /api/bookings → expect 400.

Send a direct anon PostgREST INSERT with 10 spaces in notes → expect 23514.

Send repeated burst POST /api/bookings requests → expect 429 after threshold.

Finding 5: Transient profiles DB errors misclassified as 403, unnormalized Bearer forwarding, and env-var inconsistency

Location: src/app/api/services/route.ts lines 34, 59–79; src/lib/supabaseServer.ts lines 5, 10 vs src/lib/supabase-server.ts line 9.

Attack or Failure:

In POST /api/services lines 66–80, any profileError (including a database outage or network error) falls into the same if branch as a non-provider role and returns 403 Forbidden ("A provider or merchant account is required.") instead of 503/500, misleading clients and masking outages as auth failures.

Line 34 matches /^Bearer\s+(.+)$/i and forwards the raw authorization string to PostgREST (bearer <jwt> or lowercase bearer), rather than normalizing `Bearer ${bearer[1].trim()}`.

supabaseServer.ts line 10 requires SUPABASE_URL strictly, whereas supabase-server.ts line 9 falls back to NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL (and supabaseServer.ts line 5 re-exports getSupabaseAdmin into the user-client module). If a deployment only sets NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, getSupabaseAdmin() works while /api/services and /api/bookings fail with 500.

Severity: Low (operational reliability, diagnostics, and maintainability).

Smallest Safe Fix: Handle profileError separately with a 503/500 response before checking !profile || !['provider', 'merchant'].includes(profile.role); normalize the forwarded header to `Bearer ${bearer[1].trim()}`; remove the getSupabaseAdmin re-export from supabaseServer.ts and align SUPABASE_URL ?? NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL (or document required server env vars consistently).

Verification Test (Fictional Data): Simulate a transient DB failure during the profiles query on POST /api/services with a valid fictional provider JWT and payload; verify the route returns 503/500 instead of 403.

3. Two Important Tradeoffs

Preserving Legacy profiles Rows with NOT VALID (007) vs. Strict Role Normalization

Choice made: profiles_exam_role_check uses NOT VALID so existing rows are preserved without silent rewrites, while new/updated rows are constrained to ('admin', 'merchant', 'provider', 'client').

Tradeoff: Safe against destructive migrations or breaking legacy accounts, but any existing user with a legacy role outside ('provider', 'merchant') (e.g., 'vendor') is silently denied provider actions by both /api/services and RLS until explicitly migrated, and legacy rows remain unvalidated against the new role contract.

Browser-Key Direct PostgREST Access + RLS vs. Mediated Server Writes

Choice made: Routes use createSupabaseUserClient (anon key + user JWT) and rely on GRANTs + PostgreSQL RLS as the primary security boundary (004).

Tradeoff: Eliminates service_role exposure in public/user routes and protects the database even if a Next.js handler has a bug, but because the anon key is public, clients can call PostgREST directly—bypassing API-route-only Zod rules (e.g., .trim()), route-level rate limiting, and consistent JSON error formatting unless mirrored in SQL constraints/triggers or an API gateway.

4. Evidence Missing Before Calling It Production Ready

Hosted Supabase Integration Verification: Local tests used Codex-operated local fixtures; no hosted migration, real Supabase Auth (GoTrue JWT issuance/expiry/revocation), or live PostgREST enforcement has been run.

Audit of Omitted Schema & Policies:

Lines 1–41 of 20261029140000_exam_services_persistence.sql (confirming services column defaults like coverage_active default false, CHECK constraints, and profiles schema).

Omitted sections of 20261118000400_restore_backend_contracts_rls.sql (lines 1–136, 151–178, 215–226) confirming ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on all tables, profiles SELECT/UPDATE policies, admin separation policies, and any auth.users trigger behavior.

End-to-End Lifecycle & Negative Security Tests: Automated verification against hosted/real PostgREST covering draft → approved → suspended transitions, provider reading only their own bookings via backend_booking_provider_read, and direct PostgREST negative tests (e.g., anon attempting SELECT on bookings or draft services; client attempting POST /api/services or profiles escalation).

Operational & Abuse Controls: Rate limiting / CAPTCHA on POST /api/bookings and auth endpoints, pagination on GET /api/services, environment parity verification (SUPABASE_URL, keys), structured error monitoring without PII logging, and a tested rollback/backup plan for hosted migrations.
